data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a methodological rule of 'rational action' distinct from 'inductive inference,' where corroboration reports past performance without predicting future probability, thus avoiding the smuggled induction.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the reason for preferring the survived theory relies on an expectation that it will continue to survive, induction is smuggled back in.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'rational action' cannot be defined without referencing future success probabilities, the distinction collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Semantic compartmentalization: separating the logical status of a theory (unprovable, improbable) from the pragmatic decision rule for acting on it (prefer the one that survived severe tests).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
